title: Quantum Computing Enabled ab initio Molecular Dynamics Simulations
authors: Susanta Das, Subhamoy Bhowmik, Zhen Li, Milana Bazayeva, Danil Kaliakin, Akhil Shajan, Kenneth M. Merz
abstract: We demonstrate a quantum-classical workflow for ab initio molecular dynamics (AIMD) in which quantum measurements from a chemistry-inspired LUCJ ansatz are post-processed using Sample-based Quantum Diagonalization (SQD) to recover determinant subspaces and deliver energies and analytical nuclear gradients for dynamics. As an exact benchmark, we use full configuration interaction (FCI) in the STO-3G basis, enabling a direct assessment of the accuracy of SQD. In gas-phase benchmarks, SQD reproduces FCI energies and gradients to within 1 kcal mol$^{-1}$ of the FCI reference and yields stable AIMD trajectories. In explicit-solvent QM/MM simulations, SQD retains this agreement, matching FCI energy fluctuations and RMS gradient profiles and reproducing solute-solvent structure as quantified by radial distribution functions. Overall, these benchmarks establish LUCJ+SQD as a practical route for integrating current quantum hardware into QM/MM molecular dynamics and provide an early demonstration of condensed-phase QM/MM dynamics driven by a quantum electronic-structure engine.
summary: The paper presents a novel quantum-classical workflow using Sample-based Quantum Diagonalization (SQD) to enable ab initio molecular dynamics on current quantum hardware. By benchmarking against Full CI calculations in explicit solvents, the authors demonstrate that this method accurately predicts energies and forces for QM/MM systems. This establishes a practical pathway for integrating near-term quantum processors into computational chemistry simulations.
main_problem: The primary goal is establishing a practical workflow to integrate current quantum hardware into Quantum Mechanics/Molecular Mechanics (QM/MM) molecular dynamics simulations for condensed-phase systems.
main_result: The proposed LUCJ+SQD method successfully reproduces high-accuracy Full CI energies and gradients in both gas-phase benchmarks and explicit-solvent QM/MM simulations, validating its use on quantum hardware.
method: It employs a quantum-classical workflow: quantum measurements from a LUCJ ansatz are post-processed using Sample-based Quantum Diagonalization (SQD) to estimate electronic structure properties, which are then combined with classical MM forces for dynamics.
model_or_system: The simulations model neutral solutes ($	ext{NH}_3$, $	ext{CH}_4$, $	ext{H}_2	ext{O}$) embedded in explicit liquid water. The methodology combines quantum electronic structure calculations (via SQD) with classical force fields (QM/MM framework).
key_observables: Energies, analytical nuclear gradients, and solute–solvent radial distribution functions ($	ext{RDFs}$).
important_parameters: The benchmark accuracy is set by the Full CI calculation in the STO-3G basis; performance metrics include energy deviation ($\le 1 	ext{ kcal mol}^{-1}$) and $	ext{RMS}$ gradient profile matching.
main_assumptions: The method assumes that post-processing quantum measurements via SQD can accurately recover determinant subspaces, effectively bridging current noisy hardware capabilities to high-accuracy chemical simulations.
figures_summary: Figure 1 schematically illustrates the entire QM/MM AIMD workflow, showing parallel execution paths for both the 'QUANTUM SQD BRANCH' and the 'CLASSICAL REFERENCE BRANCH' at each MD step.
paper_structure: The paper details the quantum-classical integration pipeline: first, setting up the Hamiltonian construction (Quick/PySCF); second, executing the quantum measurement via LUCJ on hardware; third, post-processing these measurements using SQD to get energies/forces; and finally, integrating these forces into an established MD engine like Amber/sander.
why_interesting: This work is highly relevant as it tackles the direct application of near-term quantum computing (NISQ) devices to complex, time-dependent many-body problems in chemistry, bridging abstract quantum algorithms with tangible molecular dynamics simulations.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Schematic of the SQD-enabled QM/MM ab initio molecular dynamics workflow integrating Amber, Quick, PySCF, and IBM quantum hardware. At each MD step, Amber/sander supplies the solute coordinates and MM point charges, from which the Quick/PySCF interface builds the electrostatically embedded QM Hamiltonian. The clas- sical reference branch uses the PySCF mcscf.CASCI kernel over the complete STO-3G orbital manifold, with all electrons active and no frozen core, and is therefore FCI in this basis. The quantum branch executes a LUCJ ansatz on ibm cleveland and post-processes the measured bitstrings by SQD. Both branches yield analytical nuclear gradients and de- fine separate...

Figure 2: Qubit layouts of the LUCJ circuits executed on ibm cleveland for (A) NH3 (10e,8o; 18 qubits), (B) CH4 (10e,9o; 21 qubits), and (C) H2O (10e,7o; 16 qubits). The device connectivity is shown in gray. Qubits used to encode spin-up and spin-down occupations are indicated in red and blue, respectively, and ancilla qubits are shown in green. The molecular structures above each layout correspond to the simulated solute; carbon, oxygen, nitrogen, and hydrogen atoms are colored gray, red, blue, and white, respectively.

Figure 3: Total electronic energy along the gas-phase NH3 trajectory in vacuum ob- tained with FCI/STO-3G reference and SQD at three SQD batch sizes (SQD200, SQD400, SQD800). The SQD curves closely overlay the FCI reference, indicating that SQD repro- duces the same potential-energy surface along the sampled path.

Figure 4: Root-mean-square (RMS) nuclear gradient magnitude along the gas-phase NH3 trajectory in vacuum obtained with FCI/STO-3G reference and SQD at three SQD batch sizes (SQD200, SQD400, SQD800). The SQD curves overlay the FCI reference across the full trajectory, indicating that SQD reproduces the force scale and its temporal modulation along the NVE path.

Figure 5: Total electronic energy (Eh) along the aqueous-phase molecular dynamics trajec- tory of NH3 in explicit water, comparing classical FCI with SQD using batch sizes N = 200, 400, and 800 samples per batch. Energies are shown as a function of simulation time (fs) with ∆t = 0.5 fs. The SQD and FCI energy traces are in excellent agreement throughout the trajectory.
